Before and After Temperature: A Distributional View of Creative LLM Generation

V.S. Raghu Parupudi Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur    Harsha Ponnada Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur    Aditi Kaushal Affiliation: Delhi Technological University    S. Shria Parupudi Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Saiteja Dasari Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur Affiliation: Rutgers University    Sahiti Bulusu Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology
Abstract

Reference-free evaluation of large language model (LLM) creativity relies on perplexity, entropy, and top-1 margin. We show that a much stronger signal lives one step earlier in the pipeline: in how sampling temperature reshapes the model’s token distribution before the next token is drawn. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct generations of 500 open-ended creative prompts at T∈{0.3,0.8,1.5}T\in\{0.3,0.8,1.5\}, a single per-token feature derived from this reshaping predicts the within-prompt creativity rank at Spearman ρ=0.918\rho{=}0.918 against an averaged gpt-4o / gemini-2.5-pro judge (n=500n{=}500) and ρ=0.870\rho{=}0.870 against a three-rater human-majority ranking (n=150n{=}150). Each of four standard reference-free baselines (self-perplexity, mean predictive entropy, top-1 margin, gzip compression ratio) tops out at |ρ|≈0.76|\rho|\!\approx\!0.76 on both ground truths: a gap of +0.165+0.165 on averaged-LLM and +0.110+0.110 on human-majority, both far larger than the spread among the baselines themselves. The two ground-truth panels agree with each other at ρ=0.83\rho{=}0.83, above the inter-human ceiling of ρ=0.77\rho{=}0.77, so the comparison is not bottlenecked by judge noise. Mechanistically, the win comes from a sharp distributional signature of the incoherence regime: at T=1.5T{=}1.5 the cumulative-mass width n95​(q)n_{95}(q) inflates from ∼1\sim\!1 to ∼131{\sim}\!131 tokens and post-temperature mass leaks off the pre-temperature top-90%90\% plausible set by about 1313 percentage points. The per-token aggregates do not separate T=0.8T{=}0.8 from T=0.3T{=}0.3; discriminating the two coherent regimes is left to sequence-level features.

Keywords: 
LLM evaluation reference-free metrics LLM-as-judge sampling temperature distributional analysis.

1 Introduction

How do we evaluate a language model’s output when there’s no reference text to compare against, as in open-ended creative generation? Perplexity is still the default [2, 11], but a generation of work has shown it falls short on open-ended tasks. Low perplexity, on its own, rewards fluent and high-frequency text. That is exactly the failure mode Holtzman et al. [10] called “neural text degeneration”. Reference-free quality metrics built on model embeddings or LLM-as-judge prompts have closed some of these gaps [27, 15, 7], but they work on the output text, not on the distribution the model produced it from.

A separate line of work treats the model’s own distribution as a signal: typicality [18], semantic entropy for hallucination detection [13, 6], self-consistency [24, 17], and learned “confidence” scores [21]. These either collapse the distribution to a scalar (entropy, perplexity, margin) or compare across multiple samples. Neither approach uses the fact that sampling temperature is itself a transformation applied to the model’s raw distribution before any token is emitted. At every generation step there are two distributions: the model’s true belief p∝exp⁡(z)p\propto\exp(z) and the temperature-reshaped distribution q∝exp⁡(z/T)q\propto\exp(z/T) from which the next token is actually sampled. The gap between pp and qq is computable from the same forward pass that produces the text.

A natural question is to ask, does the structure of this pre-vs-post temperature gap tell us how good the generation is?

We answer empirically. We generate at T∈{0.3,0.8,1.5}T\in\{0.3,0.8,1.5\} on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [8] for 500 creative prompts drawn from published sources (WritingPrompts [5], the Alternative Uses Task [9, 23], and HellaSwag [26]), capturing the raw top-KK logits at every generation step on a GCP L4 GPU (K=100K{=}100 for T≤0.8T\!\leq\!0.8, K=200K{=}200 for T=1.5T{=}1.5, with a guarantee that the sampled token is always in the captured set).

Our findings, ordered by what we think matters most: (i) a single per-token feature derived from the pre-vs-post temperature reshape correlates with the within-prompt creativity rank at ρ=0.918\rho{=}0.918 against an averaged LLM judge and ρ=0.870\rho{=}0.870 against the human majority, beating each of four standard reference-free baselines by more than 0.100.10 in absolute ρ\rho on both ground truths; (ii) the underlying mechanism is a sharp distributional signature of the incoherence regime (n95​(q)n_{95}(q) inflation, ∼13{\sim}13-pp mass leakage off the pre-temperature top-90%90\% plausible set); and (iii) per-token aggregates do not separate T=0.8T{=}0.8 from T=0.3T{=}0.3, which we read as a pointer toward sequence-level features for that finer distinction rather than as a limitation of the pre-vs-post view itself.

2 Related Work

Reference-free quality metrics.

Perplexity [2, 11] is still widely used as a quality stand-in, even though its problems are well known. Holtzman et al. [10] showed that minimising perplexity drives “neural text degeneration”: bland, repetitive output that hits a fluency target while saying nothing. Fabbri et al. [4] found that perplexity-class metrics correlate weakly with human quality judgements on summarisation. Reference-based n-gram metrics like BLEU [20] simply do not apply when there is no reference. Embedding-based reference-free signals such as BARTScore [25] and BERTScore variants [27] have filled that gap for open-ended tasks, but they score the surface form of the output, not the distribution that produced it. Our work targets that second layer directly.

LLM-as-judge.

A second strand of work treats evaluation as a generation task in its own right: prompt a strong LLM to score or rank candidates. G-Eval [15] and GPTScore [7] are the canonical examples; Prometheus [12] is an open-weight judge in the same family. These judges correlate well with humans on many tasks but can over-reward fluent incoherence when an answer opens strongly and falls apart later; Chakrabarty et al. [3] report this failure mode on long-form creative writing. We use a coherence-first ranking prompt to control for it (Section 3.5).

Model-internal uncertainty.

A third line of work mines the generating model’s own distribution for signal. Predictive entropy and margin-based confidence are the classical handles [16]. Semantic entropy [13] clusters multiple sampled completions by meaning, and the same idea drives hallucination detection [6]. Locally typical decoding [18] is the closest in spirit to what we do: it treats each token’s deviation from expected surprisal as a signal, but uses it to pick tokens during sampling rather than to evaluate afterwards. Self-consistency [24] and SelfCheckGPT [17] use agreement across multiple samples, which works but multiplies inference cost. All of these methods collapse the distribution to a scalar or compare across samples. None of them looks at the structure of how temperature itself reshapes the distribution at a single step.

Diversity and degeneration.

Corpus-level diversity has been measured with distinct-nn [14], self-BLEU [28], and compression-ratio variants [22, 19]. These tools tell you how varied a sample set is in aggregate. They cannot tell you anything about the per-token shape of the distribution behind any single response, which is the level we operate at. We include compression ratio as one of our sequence-level baselines (Section 5.4) precisely because it tests whether surface diversity alone explains what our distributional features pick up. It does not.

Temperature as a study variable.

Prior decoding work (nucleus [10], typical [18]) notes that the tail behaves differently at high TT, but does not quantify the pre-vs-post reshape itself. That is the question we set out to answer.

3 Experimental Setup

3.1 Prompts

We select 500 open-ended creative prompts (English, 15–250 characters, no single-answer items) from three published sources: WritingPrompts [5] (168 story starters from r/WritingPrompts, filtered for self-contained prompts); the Alternative Uses Task [9, 23] (166 “list creative uses for XX” prompts, the standard divergent-thinking instrument); and the HellaSwag ActivityNet split [26] (166 scene-continuation prompts of the form “continue this scene in a vivid, imaginative way”). All sources are licensed for research use.

3.2 Model and Generation

We generate all samples with meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [8] in fp16, on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU (24 GB VRAM) on Google Cloud Platform.

For each prompt we generate three independent autoregressive traces, one at each T∈{0.3,0.8,1.5}T\in\{0.3,0.8,1.5\}, with max_new_tokens=300{=}300 and the model’s default chat template. Contexts diverge from step 1 onward; we do not share traces across temperatures.

3.3 Logit Capture

For each generated token, we record the top-KK raw logits (token id and logit value) before any sampling. The capture depth is a function of temperature:

  • •

    T∈{0.3,0.8}T\in\{0.3,0.8\}: K=100K{=}100. The post-temperature distribution is highly peaked, and the top-100 captures ≥0.99\geq 0.99 of the mass for virtually all positions.

  • •

    T=1.5T=1.5: K=200K{=}200. The post-temperature distribution is much flatter; we need a wider head to retain ≥0.95\geq 0.95 of the mass for stable divergence computation.

We additionally guarantee that the sampled token is always in the recorded list (appended if it lay outside top-KK), so that chosen-token analyses remain well-defined at high TT. The append rate (Table 1) jumps roughly 1000×1000\times from T=0.8T{=}0.8 to T=1.5T{=}1.5, confirming that K=200K{=}200 at T=1.5T{=}1.5 is reasonable but tight and that the append is load-bearing.

3.4 Two Distributions per Token

We now have access to the raw logits zz (top-KK) at each generated token of each trace. From these we calculate on the renormalised top-KK head:

  • •

    Pre-temperature distribution: p=softmax⁡(z)p=\mathrm{softmax}(z), the model’s untouched belief about next-token candidates at this position.

  • •

    Post-temperature distribution: q=softmax⁡(z/T)q=\mathrm{softmax}(z/T), the temperature-reshaped distribution from which the actual sampled token was drawn.

At T=1T{=}1 exactly, p≡qp{\equiv}q and every divergence vanishes; we exclude it from the main grid for that reason, and exclude T=0T{=}0 because greedy decoding degenerated visibly. The construction is identical across all three temperatures, so within-trace and within-prompt comparisons are exact. We use divergences only to rank prompts and traces relative to each other, not against any external benchmark.

3.5 Ground Truth

We use two independent layers of ground truth.

LLM-judge ensemble (full 500 prompts).

For every prompt, we present its three responses to two judges from different model families: gpt-4o [1] (via the OpenAI API) and gemini-2.5-pro (via Google Vertex AI). The judge prompt is identical across the two models. It asks for a three-way ranking by creativity with ties allowed, explicitly penalizes incoherence, code-switching, and disconnected technical jargon, and instructs the judge to read the whole response rather than just the opening. The presentation order of the three responses is randomly shuffled per prompt (seeded), so position bias is averaged out across the corpus. Each judge produces 500 rankings.

Human raters (150-prompt subset).

The first 150 prompts (56 WP, 48 HellaSwag, 46 AUT) were ranked by three independent raters, co-authors of this paper, working blind to temperature labels and without communicating during annotation, under the same coherence-first rule as the LLM judges and a fixed A/B/C presentation order so judgements are directly comparable. Inter-rater agreement is reported in Section 5.1.

4 Distributional Metrics

Given the per-token pre- and post-temperature distributions pp and qq from Section 3.4, we compute a set of measures, each capturing a different aspect of how temperature reshapes the distribution. They fall into five families.

4.1 Information-Theoretic Divergences

  • •

    KL(q∥p)=∑iqilog(qi/pi)\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\sum_{i}q_{i}\log(q_{i}/p_{i}): post-to-pre Kullback–Leibler divergence.

  • •

    KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q): the reverse direction. At T=0T{=}0 this blows up to +∞+\infty because qq is one-hot. We do not use T=0T{=}0 in the main grid, but we keep the metric to expose the asymmetry.

  • •

    JS(p,q)=12KL(p∥m)+12KL(q∥m)\mathrm{JS}(p,q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}(p\|m)+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}(q\|m) with m=(p+q)/2m=(p+q)/2: Jensen–Shannon, symmetric and bounded.

4.2 Geometric Distances

  • •

    Total variation: TV⁡(p,q)=12​∑i|pi−qi|\mathrm{TV}(p,q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}|p_{i}-q_{i}|.

  • •

    L2L_{2}: ∑i(pi−qi)2\sqrt{\sum_{i}(p_{i}-q_{i})^{2}}.

  • •

    Hellinger: 12​∑i(pi−qi)2\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{i}(\sqrt{p_{i}}-\sqrt{q_{i}})^{2}}.

4.3 Top-end Properties

  • •

    Top-1 probability under pre and post: maxi⁡pi\max_{i}p_{i}, maxi⁡qi\max_{i}q_{i}.

  • •

    Top-1 shift: maxi⁡qi−maxi⁡pi\max_{i}q_{i}-\max_{i}p_{i}. Positive at T<1T\!<\!1 (sharpening promotes the leader), negative at T>1T\!>\!1 (flattening demotes it).

  • •

    Top-1 identity change: indicator that the arg⁡max\arg\max differs between pp and qq.

  • •

    Margin: p(1)−p(2)p_{(1)}-p_{(2)} (and the same for qq).

4.4 Chosen-Token Properties

At each step we record the token that was actually sampled. By construction it sits in the captured top-KK (Section 3.3).

  • •

    p⁡[chosen]p[\text{chosen}]: the pre-temperature probability of the sampled token, i.e. how plausible was this pick on the raw distribution? High values mean the chosen token was already a leader; low values mean temperature promoted a long-tail candidate.

  • •

    q⁡[chosen]q[\text{chosen}]: the post-temperature probability of the sampled token.

4.5 Cumulative-Mass Width and Mass Leakage

Two complementary measures of how temperature spreads mass across candidates.

Top-nαn_{\alpha} width.

For threshold α∈{0.90,0.95,0.99}\alpha\in\{0.90,0.95,0.99\}, nα​(p)n_{\alpha}(p) is the smallest number of top-ranked tokens whose probability sums to at least α\alpha. We compute nα​(p)n_{\alpha}(p) and nα​(q)n_{\alpha}(q) at every step. The signed difference nα​(q)−nα​(p)n_{\alpha}(q)-n_{\alpha}(p) is the flattening: positive when temperature spreads mass into more candidates, negative when it concentrates.

When the captured top-KK head sums to less than α\alpha, which only happens at T=1.5T{=}1.5 for α=0.99\alpha{=}0.99 on a small fraction of positions, we mark nαn_{\alpha} as censored at KK and drop those positions from analyses that need an uncensored value.

Mass leakage.

Let Sα(p)S_{\alpha}^{(p)} be the set of tokens that make up pp’s top-nα​(p)n_{\alpha}(p) mass, i.e. the “pre-temperature α\alpha-plausible set”. Then:

PostCumOnPreα=∑i∈Sα(p)qi.\textsc{PostCumOnPre}_{\alpha}\;=\;\sum_{i\in S_{\alpha}^{(p)}}q_{i}. (1)

This is the post-temperature mass that stays on the original plausible set. Anchor values:

  • •

    At T=1T{=}1 it equals α\alpha by construction.

  • •

    At T<1T{<}1 it rises toward 11: sharpening pushes more mass onto the original leaders.

  • •

    At T>1T{>}1 it falls below α\alpha: flattening leaks mass off the originally-plausible set and onto the tail.

The symmetric quantity PreCumOnPostα=∑i∈Sα(q)pi\textsc{PreCumOnPost}_{\alpha}=\sum_{i\in S_{\alpha}^{(q)}}p_{i} tells us the other direction: how much pre-temperature mass was already on the set that ended up plausible under temperature. Together they describe the redistribution.

4.6 Per-Response Aggregation

Each trace has about 290290 rows in the per-token table. For each metric we aggregate per (prompt, TT) using mean, median, p10, p90, max, plus min for the chosen-token measures (which catches the least-plausible commitment). We use multiple aggregators on purpose: the same divergence looks different at the typical-token vs. worst-token level, and Section 5.3 shows that the p10\mathrm{p10} aggregator (calmest position in the trace) is often the strongest single signal.

4.7 Audit of Degenerate Metrics

Top-1 identity change is always 00 within a step (rank-invariance); nαn_{\alpha} censoring is 0%0\% at α∈{0.90,0.95}\alpha\in\{0.90,0.95\} for our chosen KK; KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) at T=0T{=}0 is undefined. The analysis in Section 5 excludes these; the full pre-audit catalogue is available on request.

5 Results

5.1 Ground-Truth Rankings

LLM judge ensemble.

Both gpt-4o and gemini-2.5-pro parsed cleanly on all 500 prompts. Figure 1(a) shows the mean rank each judge assigned to each temperature. gpt-4o ranked T=0.8{=}0.8 first on 293 prompts and T=0.3{=}0.3 first on 217 (counts include ties at the top, so they sum to more than 500). For gemini-2.5-pro the corresponding counts are 321 and 248. Neither judge ranked T=1.5{=}1.5 first on more than one prompt out of 500. Both produce an inverted-U: T=0.8{=}0.8 wins on a majority of prompts, T=0.3{=}0.3 is close behind, and T=1.5{=}1.5 is ranked last on 499/500499/500 (gpt-4o) and 500/500500/500 (gemini-2.5-pro) prompts.

Judge-judge agreement, measured as the mean Spearman rank correlation across the three temperatures within each prompt, is ρ=+0.794\rho{=}+0.794 (median +0.866+0.866). The judges are in lockstep at the bottom of the ranking and disagree only on the bland-vs-mid ordering at the top.

Human raters.

On the 150-prompt subset, three independent raters ranked the responses under the same coherence-first rule as the LLM judges. Two raters finished all 150 items; Rater 3 finished 147. Figure 1(b) shows mean rank per temperature for each rater and for their mean-rank majority. All three raters ranked T=1.5{=}1.5 last on essentially every item (rater means ≈3.00\approx 3.00). T=0.3{=}0.3 and T=0.8{=}0.8 are within 0.050.05 rank units of each other for every rater, which means the mid-vs-bland call is the closer one even for humans.

Inter-rater agreement, measured per-prompt as Spearman across the three temperatures, is ρ=+0.798\rho{=}+0.798 (Rater 1 vs Rater 3), ρ=+0.761\rho{=}+0.761 (Rater 1 vs Rater 2), and ρ=+0.755\rho{=}+0.755 (Rater 2 vs Rater 3). The average is ρ=+0.771\rho{=}+0.771, which we take as the human-agreement ceiling for this task.

5.2 Human-vs-LLM Agreement

We compare each LLM judge, and their average, against the human-majority ranking on the 150-prompt subset (Figure 2; Rater 3’s 3 unranked items are excluded from pairs involving Rater 3).

The averaged-LLM judge clears the inter-human ceiling (ρ=+0.832\rho{=}+0.832 vs. +0.771+0.771), so the LLM judges are noisy but unbiased estimators of the same construct as the humans. Gemini-2.5-pro aligns marginally better with humans than gpt-4o (+0.803+0.803 vs. +0.793+0.793), so it is the safer single-judge proxy, but the averaged judge is what we use for the headline distributional analyses in Section 5.3.

5.3 The Incoherence Signature

We rank-correlate every per-response aggregated feature (Section 4) against (a) the averaged-LLM rank per (prompt,TT) on all 500 prompts, and (b) the human-majority rank on the 150-prompt subset. For each feature we report the within-prompt Spearman ρ\rho across the three temperatures, averaged across all prompts with at least two distinct feature values.

Figure 3 brings together the per-TT mean values for every metric we examine in this section: our distributional features in the top two rows, and the four literature baselines we compare against in Section 5.4 in the bottom row. Every distributional feature cleanly separates T=1.5T{=}1.5 from the other two temperatures, often by one to three orders of magnitude, and Table 2 translates that separation into Spearman correlations against the averaged-LLM ground truth.

Table 2 ranks the same distributional features by how strongly they correlate with the averaged-LLM ground truth, alongside their correlation against the human-majority ranking on the 150-prompt subset. Within-prompt ρ\rho measures how reliably a single feature value predicts the three-temperature ranking on a given prompt.

Mass leakage off the plausible set.

postCumOnPre90\textsc{postCumOnPre}_{90} is the fraction of post-temperature mass that stays on the pre-temperature top-90%90\% set (Figure 3, postCumOnPre90 mean panel). It sits at 1.0001.000 at T=0.3T{=}0.3 and 0.9820.982 at T=0.8T{=}0.8, then drops to 0.8680.868 at T=1.5T{=}1.5. The drop is not gradual: T=0.3T{=}0.3 and T=0.8T{=}0.8 are nearly indistinguishable, then T=1.5T{=}1.5 is a step away. Temperature at T=1.5T{=}1.5 leaks about 1313 pp of the mass off the model’s own pre-temperature plausible candidates onto tokens outside that set.

5.4 Comparison Against Four Literature Baselines

We compute four canonical reference-free baselines on the same 1500 traces and the same renormalised top-KK head: self-perplexity [11]; mean post-temperature predictive entropy of the chosen-token distribution [16]; mean top-1 margin q(1)−q(2)q_{(1)}{-}q_{(2)}; and compression ratio |gzip⁡(text)|/|text||\mathrm{gzip}(\text{text})|/|\text{text}| [22, 19], the only sequence-level baseline. Per-TT means for all four are in the bottom row of Figure 3; their rank correlations against each ground truth, alongside our distributional features, are in Figure 4.

All four baselines cluster tightly: Δ​ρ<0.01\Delta\rho{<}0.01 on the averaged-LLM panel and Δ​ρ=0.026\Delta\rho{=}0.026 on human-majority (Figure 4, right panel). Our top distributional feature beats the best baseline by +0.165+0.165 (0.9180.918 vs. 0.7530.753) against the averaged-LLM judge and by +0.110+0.110 (0.8700.870 vs. 0.7600.760) against the human majority.

5.5 Where the Per-Token View Saturates

The headline correlations above are driven by the clean T=1.5T{=}1.5-vs-rest separation. The finer mid-vs-bland distinction (T=0.8T{=}0.8 vs T=0.3T{=}0.3) sits closer to the limit of what any single per-token feature in our catalogue can resolve, and the literature baselines do not resolve it either. For our top feature n90​(p)n_{90}(p)__p10 the per-TT mean is identical at T=0.3T{=}0.3 and T=0.8T{=}0.8 (1.01.0 at both); for self-perplexity it shifts modestly (1.191.19 vs. 1.921.92); meanwhile the gap from either to T=1.5T{=}1.5 is one to three orders of magnitude on every metric. The signal that distinguishes the two coherent regimes appears to live at the sequence level (which content the model commits to over the trajectory) rather than in how individual next-token distributions are shaped at any one step. We return to this in Section 6.

6 Discussion

6.1 Why the Pre-vs-Post View Beats Single-Temperature Scalars

The headline finding ρ=0.918\rho{=}0.918 against the averaged LLM judge and ρ=0.870\rho{=}0.870 against the human majority, versus |ρ|≈0.76|\rho|\!\approx\!0.76 for every literature baseline we tested, is not a small effect. The four baselines cluster within Δ​ρ<0.01\Delta\rho{<}0.01 of each other on averaged-LLM and within Δ​ρ=0.026\Delta\rho{=}0.026 on human-majority; our top feature beats the best of them by +0.165+0.165 and +0.110+0.110 respectively, i.e. a margin many times larger than the inter-baseline spread on either panel. Self-perplexity, predictive entropy, top-1 margin, and gzip compression ratio each collapse the same generation to a single scalar; they cannot see that the temperature transform z↦z/Tz\mapsto z/T reshapes the distribution before sampling. The pre-vs-post view does see this, from the same forward pass, with no extra inference cost.

The win comes from a mechanism the baselines structurally cannot access. Across our measures (KL, TV, Hellinger, top-1-prob shift, nαn_{\alpha} width, mass leakage), the T=1.5T{=}1.5 generations sit far from T=0.3T{=}0.3 and T=0.8T{=}0.8 in distributional feature space, and the shift is uniform across the trace: even the 10th-percentile position moves sharply, not just occasional outliers. The cleanest quantification is the per-token mass leakage off the pre-temperature top-90%90\% plausible set, which drops from 0.9820.982 at T=0.8T{=}0.8 to 0.8680.868 at T=1.5T{=}1.5 (a ∼13{\sim}13-percentage-point leak). The tail of the model’s belief carries enough mass at T=1.5T{=}1.5 that the sampled tokens are no longer recognisable continuations of the prompt’s context, qualitatively consistent with the typicality framing of Meister et al. [18] and the nucleus-sampling intuition [10].

6.2 Scope of the Per-Token View

The pre-vs-post view’s strongest signal is at the incoherence boundary. The mid-vs-bland gap (T=0.8T{=}0.8 vs T=0.3T{=}0.3), where both LLM and human judges find the distinction subtle, sits closer to the limit of what any single per-token statistic can resolve: at T=0.3T{=}0.3 and T=0.8T{=}0.8, pp and qq preserve roughly the same shape at every position, so the signal lives instead in which token gets sampled at flat-distribution positions, whose effect compounds over the trajectory. This points toward sequence-level features (n-gram diversity, content novelty, self-similarity across samples) as a complementary layer to the per-token catalogue, not as a replacement for it.

6.3 Implications for Reference-Free Metric Design

A creativity-aware, reference-free metric was proposed in an earlier version of this work [21] using a hand-designed scalar (chosen-token probability times the top-NN standard deviation). The results here suggest that the “one scalar per response” framing may be too crude. Information about the temperature regime is layered: which features change, by how much, and at which positions of the trace. Different aggregators carry the signal for different feature families: p10 (the calmest position) for the cumulative-mass-width levels, max (the single most-perturbed position) for the flattening difference, and p90 (the most-perturbed position) for the signed entropy shift and preCumOnPost (Table 2). A single scalar collapses that structure away.

7 Limitations

Single model.

All distributional analysis is on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [8]. On the mechanistic argument (temperature transform + tail-mass redistribution is architecture-agnostic) we expect qualitative replication on other architectures.

Top-KK truncation.

All divergences are computed on the renormalised top-KK head, pp and qq are both probability distributions over the same KK captured tokens. This is exact (no estimation) and consistent across all three temperatures, so comparisons within-prompt and within-TT are apples-to-apples. However, we do not report absolute divergence magnitudes against any external benchmark.

Single-pass measurement.

We measure pp and qq from a single forward pass per generated token; we do not, for example, run the model multiple times to characterise sampling variance in the distribution itself. This is a conscious choice (single-pass is cheap and matches deployment), but it means we can’t decompose the residual variance into "the model is uncertain about pp here" vs "pp is sharp but the trace diverges from baseline anyway".

8 Conclusion

We studied reference-free evaluation of open-ended LLM generation by treating the distributional shift caused by sampling temperature as the primary observable. This let us ask not “how confident was the model?” but “how far did temperature push the sampling distribution away from the model’s own belief, and where?”.

  1. 1.

    A single per-token feature derived from the pre-vs-post temperature reshape beats every standard reference-free baseline on both ground truths. The top feature predicts the within-prompt creativity rank at Spearman ρ=0.918\rho{=}0.918 against an averaged LLM judge and ρ=0.870\rho{=}0.870 against the human majority; the best of self-perplexity, predictive entropy, top-1 margin, and gzip compression ratio tops out at |ρ|≈0.76|\rho|\!\approx\!0.76 on both panels. The pre-vs-post divergence catalogue is a cheap, qualitatively interpretable single-pass measurement that requires no reference text and avoids the multi-sample cost of methods like semantic entropy [13].

  2. 2.

    The mechanism is a sharp distributional signature of the incoherence regime. At T=1.5T{=}1.5, mass on the pre-temperature top-90%90\% plausible set drops from 0.9820.982 at T=0.8T{=}0.8 to 0.8680.868 (a ∼13{\sim}13-percentage-point leak), and n95​(q)n_{95}(q) inflates by an order of magnitude. The distortion is uniform across the trace, not confined to occasional “creative” tokens.

  3. 3.

    Per-token aggregates do not separate T=0.8T{=}0.8 from T=0.3T{=}0.3. The mid-vs-bland distinction lives at the sequence level (which token gets sampled at flat-distribution positions, compounded over the trajectory) and is a natural target for sequence-level features rather than a limit of the pre-vs-post view itself.

Future directions.

Two immediate extensions: (a) test the pre-vs-post catalogue on other model families (Mistral, Qwen, larger Llama) to check whether the incoherence signature is architecture-agnostic, as the mechanistic argument suggests; and (b) run a finer temperature sweep on a smaller prompt subset to characterise the T=0.8→T=1.5T{=}0.8\to T{=}1.5 transition more precisely.
